newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to reorganise food safety services.
newsitem.headline: EU to reorganise food safety services.

text.p: The European Commission, anxious to avoid being censured by the European Parliament which says it seriously mishandled the mad cow crisis, will announce major changes in its public and animal health services on Wednesday.

Political groups in the parliament are preparing censure motions for the assembly's debate on February 19 of a highly critical report from its committee of inquiry into the disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
A censure motion, if it gains the required two-thirds majority of votes cast, would force Commission President Jacques Santer and his 19 colleagues to resign.

"It's a very political matter. It's normal to debate the issue in Parliament," the Commission's chief spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas said on Tuesday, adding that full details of the changes will be reserved until next week.
Last month Santer promised the inquiry that he would make sweeping changes, notably by appointing the EU's consumer affairs commissioner Emma Bonino to look after public and animal health.

The Commission's powerful agriculture directorate general, which formerly drafted, implemented and monitored BSE measures, has been criticised for giving priority to protecting beef producers' incomes over public health.
The reorganisation is also expected to include plans for an independent food safety agency, outlined by Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler in December.

It would be modelled on the EU's financial watchdog, the Court of Auditors, rather than the United States Food and Drug Administration, officials said, pointing out that the American agency did not cover meat.
But EU member states are reluctant to give up control in such a sensitive area or provide the necessary funds.
The Commission is also expected to announce measures to improve its network of scientific advisory committees by making them more professional and politically independent.
But it is unlikely to satisfy the parliament, which is fuming at its inability to take direct legal action against the British government which it sees as the main culprit.

A British government admission last March that BSE could be transmitted to humans who ate infected beef was the spark that ignited the crisis, shattering consumer confidence and undermining the beef market.
Parliament is likely to press Santer to go further and sanction senior Commission officials responsible for mistakes over BSE.
While denying that any heads would roll, the Commission said there could be some staff changes.
"It's obvious that if administrative reforms are made, people will be moved," Van der Pas said.
